case_prompt:
A 61-year-old previously healthy male was transferred to the emergency department of a tertiary referral center in South Korea during the summer season due to a 10-day history of recurrent high fever. Four days prior to transfer, he developed progressive orthopnea and oliguria. Epidemiological history revealed that approximately 20 days prior to presentation, he had sat on an outdoor lawn for several hours.

On physical examination, the patient was in moderate respiratory distress. Pulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral fine inspiratory crackles. Dermatological examination revealed an asymptomatic 1 x 1 cm erythematous to black-colored ulcerative lesion covered with a dark adherent crust on his scrotum. In addition, an erythematous maculopapular eruption was diffusely distributed across his trunk and back.

Laboratory evaluation demonstrated a white blood cell count of 9,800/uL with marked neutrophilic predominance (93.1%), C-reactive protein of 28.59 mg/dL, procalcitonin of 30 ng/mL, and serum creatinine elevated to 2.84 mg/dL (up from a baseline of 1.1 mg/dL recorded 4 days earlier). A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with slight ST-segment depression in leads V5 and V6, and cardiac troponin T was elevated at 0.231 ng/mL (reference < 0.005 ng/mL). Plain chest radiography showed multifocal patchy haziness throughout both lungs. Emergency transthoracic echocardiography revealed focal hypokinesis of the basal, basoinferior, and mid-to-basal inferolateral segments with mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 45%) and normal left ventricular wall thickness.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Coronary Syndrome (Non-ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to chest symptoms, ischemic ST depressions in lateral leads (V5-V6), progressive troponin elevation (rising to 9.383 ng/mL), and regional wall motion abnormalities, but ruled out by urgent coronary angiography demonstrating widely patent coronary arteries.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Because the progression of myocarditis was suspected, endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) from the RV and coronary angiography (CAG) was performed 4 h later. Coronary angiography did not show any significant lesion.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Viral or Autoimmune Fulminant Myocarditis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered following rapid deterioration into refractory cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest requiring VA-ECMO, and endomyocardial biopsy demonstrating lymphocytic myocarditis, but comprehensive testing for common cardiotropic viruses and autoimmune antibodies was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Other tests for viral or autoimmune etiologies were negative. Acute fulminant myocarditis caused by scrub typhus was confirmed.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Scrub Typhus with Fulminant Myocarditis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Clinically suspected based on the pathognomonic scrotal eschar, maculopapular rash, and lawn exposure despite the unseasonal summer presentation; confirmed by whole-blood nested PCR detecting the 56-kDa gene of Orientia tsutsugamushi (Ikeda strain), endomyocardial biopsy confirming CD3+/CD5+ T-lymphocytic infiltration, and dramatic hemodynamic and functional recovery supported by VA-ECMO, azithromycin, and doxycycline.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: During VA-ECMO treatment, we obtained the positive result of PCR for O. tsutsugamushi... A size of 483 bp product was obtained by nested PCR on a part of the 56 kDa gene of O. tsutsugamushi. Ikeda strain of O. tsutsugamushi was detected by DNA sequencing (GenBank accession number AP008981). Endomyocardial biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltration in myocardium and interstitium which is compatible with myocarditis with T-lymphocytic infiltration (Figures 4A,B) with positive staining for CD3 and CD5 and negative for CD 20.

editor_comments: Distilled according to Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Zero spoilers or pathogen names in admission case prompt. Catheterization, ECMO, endomyocardial biopsy, and nested PCR held until diagnostic reasoning.
